paragraph.content: Christine Hua, MD - 12/14/2025 12:24 PM PST

item.content:
Formatting of this note might be different from the original.
Please have the staples in your scalp removed in 7-10 days (around 12/21)
You can have this done by your primary care doctor, or if not then at urgent care, and if not there then the emergency department
Diagnosis/Evaluation:
Today, you were seen for syncope (passing out) and head injury. We did CT scan, X-rays, Ultrasound, Lab tests, and EKG that showed no emergent findings. Based on your workup here in the emergency department, you were deemed stable for discharge.
Follow Up:
Please follow up with your primary care doctor in the next 2-5 days or sooner if needed
Medications:
Continue your home medications as previously prescribed.
Please return to the emergency department if you experience ANY of the following:
Severe worsening headache, persistent nausea/vomiting, vision changes, confusion, more episodes of passing out/losing consciousness
Fevers
Chest pain
Trouble breathing
Sudden weakness or numbness
ANY new or worsening symptoms that are concerning to you!
If you are in need of a primary care provider please see below:
UCI Health: Appointments - Family Health Center (FHC)
To schedule an initial or follow-up appointment with the FHC Anaheim offices, just call (657) 282-6356 and we will assist you through the process.
The FHC Anaheim offices are located at:
300 W Carl Karcher Way
Anaheim, CA 92801
The FHC Santa Ana medical offices are located at:
FHC Santa Ana Clinic
800 N. Main Street
Santa Ana, CA 92701
Please note: For UCI clinics and physicians other than the emergency department, your health insurance provider may or may not require prior authorization before an appointment at UCI can be made on your behalf. If you are not sure whether or not your health insurance company requires prior authorization, please call your health insurance provider first to prevent any unnecessary delays in your care.

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Chief Complaint
Patient presents with
Syncope
BIBA from Theo Lacy s/p syncopal episode. +laceration to occipital area.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
Interpreter used: No (English Preferred Language)
Anthony Michael Dimarcello is a 42 years old male with no significant pmhx brought in by ambulance from Theo Lacy s/p syncope and head injury.
Patient states he was urinating when he had sudden onset dizziness and then syncopized, falling and hitting his posterior head on the ground. Per EMS: patient hypotensive on scene, BP 80s/60s, which improved on route after administration of IV fluids. Patient currently denies any symptoms. Denies chest pain, shortness of breath, cough, fever, abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, dizziness, paresthesias, or headache. Not on anticoagulants.
PMH/SHx/Allgs/FHx/Shx/SDOH:
History reviewed. No pertinent past medical history.
There are no active problems to display for this patient.

none

VITAL SIGNS:
First Vitals [12/14/25 1116]
Temp Pulse Resp BP SpO2
36.7 °C (98 °F) 62 16 116/79 99 %
Physical Exam
General: Awake, alert, in no apparent distress.
HEENT: Normocephalic, +3cm laceration to left occipital scalp. PERRL, EOMI, moist mucous membranes.
Neck: Negative C-spine ttp, c-collar in place.
Respiratory: Lungs CTAB, no wheezing, no crackles. Breathing comfortably and in no respiratory distress.
Cardiovascular: RRR, no obvious murmurs. Extremities are warm and well perfused.
Abdomen: Soft, nontender, nondistended, no rebound/guarding.
Back: Negative midline T/L-spine ttp.
Extremities: No LE edema, clubbing, or cyanosis. No tenderness to joints or extremities.
Neuro: Awake and alert. Moving extremities. No focal neuro deficits. Clear speech.
Psych: Answers questions appropriately.
MEDICAL DECISION MAKING
Initial Impressions:
Anthony Michael Dimarcello is a 42 years old male who presents with syncope and fall with head injury.
Vital signs and physical exam were notable for: Afebrile, nontachycardic, normotensive, saturating appropriately on room air. Exam with 3cm occipital scalp laceration, no focal neuro deficits, rest of exam unremarkable.
Differential diagnosis includes: vasovagal syncope, orthostatics given hypotension reported in field, dehydration, electrolyte derangement, lower suspicion for ICH, exam and history not consistent with seizure given no seizure-like activity no postictal state, low suspicion for acute underlying infection given no fever no cough no reported infectious symptoms
Workup Review:
Pertinent Lab Results (interpreted independently by me): CBC with no leukocytosis doubt severe systemic infection, no anemia doubt severe hemorrhage as cause of symptoms, no thrombocytopenia. CMP with no major electrolyte derangements, no AKI. Serial troponins negative x3.
Pertinent Imaging Results (interpreted independently by me):
- CT head negative for acute ICH or skull fracture
- CT C-spine negative for acute fracture
- Chest XR negative for obvious focal consolidation, pleural effusion, or large pneumothorax per my read
EKG (interpreted independently by me): sinus rhythm at 62 bpm, normal axis, normal intervals, no evidence of acute ischemic changes
Patient here after syncopal episode with collapse and head injury. Had preceding symptoms of dizziness, no other chest pain or shortness of breath. Was noted to be hypotensive in the field, which rapidly improved on reassessment and after fluid bolus and has remained stable. On arrival to ED, patient awake alert mentating appropriately with no focal neuro deficits. Small occipital scalp laceration cleaned and repaired with staples x6, patient tolerated procedure well. CT imaging negative for any acute traumatic findings. Labs overall unremarkable. TEE obtained with LV EF 52%, no other abnormal findings. Serial troponins negative x3 and nonischemic EKG, doubt ACS. Patient observed for quite some time in the emergency department with no further episodes of syncope or acute decompensation. Patient ambulated and tolerated PO. Discussed with him all results and plan for close PCP follow-up. Strict return precautions provided. He verbalized understanding and was amenable with plan of care, hemodynamically stable and symptomatically improved upon discharge back to facility.
Disposition Decision:
Discharge
Patient's exam and workup were reassuring. They are stable for discharge at this time and I recommend that they pursue outpatient follow up for their complaint. Questions answered and return precautions provided.
There are no discharge medications for this patient.
